## Abstract

Gene delivery vehicles based on adeno-associated viruses (AAV) are enabling increasing success in human clinical trials and offer the promise of treating a broad spectrum of both genetic and non-genetic disorders. However, delivery efficiency and targeting must be improved to enable safe and effective therapies. In recent years, considerable effort has been invested to create AAV variants with improved delivery, and computational approaches have been increasingly harnessed for AAV engineering. Here, we discuss how computationally designed AAV libraries are enabling directed evolution. Specifically, we highlight approaches that harness sequences outputted by next generation sequencing coupled with machine learning to generate new functional AAV capsids and related regulatory elements, pushing the frontier of what vector engineering and gene therapy may achieve.

## AAV Engineering for Developing Clinical Gene Therapy

Gene therapy is the delivery of genetic material to a patient to correct, augment, or inhibit a biological function for treating a disease. The efficacy of such treatments has typically hinged on the efficiency and specificity of the delivery vehicle[1]. Among the many vehicles that have advanced from the bench to the clinic (e.g., treating retinal disease and spinal muscular atrophy etc.), adeno-associated viral (AAV) vectors have risen to prominence due to their unique attributes. In particular, natural AAVs can transduce post-mitotic cells with moderate efficiency, have low to no genotoxicity due to a predominantly non-integrating genome, and lack known pathogenicity[2]. Over the past two decades, over 136 clinical trials have used AAVs[3], and to date the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved five AAV-based gene therapies for diseases in the retina, central nervous system (CNS), blood system, and muscle (Table 1)[4–6]. These successes have been enabled by the infectivity of naturally occurring AAV serotypes, boosted by large dosages and/or invasive routes of administration; however, their properties are likely insufficient to safely and effectively treat the majority of human diseases. As a result, new AAVs that are more efficient, ideally mediate cell- or tissue-specific delivery, and have low interactions with the immune system will be needed for treating most disorders[7].

Library selection and directed evolution-based AAV vector engineering, involving the development of genetically diverse AAV library pools followed by single round or iterative selection for improved function (i.e. cell-specific delivery), have enabled the engineering of substantially improved vectors, a number of which have recently advanced into the clinic[8,9]. Additionally, the parallel emergence of next-generation sequencing (NGS) paired with computational analysis and machine learning applications have increasingly enhanced AAV capsid engineering efforts. This review begins with a brief overview of the original methodologies for AAV library construction and screening. It then discusses how AAV capsid and regulatory element library design facilitated by the synergy between computational science and biological engineering is further empowering the evolution of AAV-based gene therapies.

## AAV Capsid Diversification and Directed Evolution

AAV was first encountered as a contaminant in adenoviral stocks in 1965 and later classified as a member of Dependovirus genus within the Paroviridae family[10]. The wildtype AAV genome consists of single-stranded, 4.8 kilobase DNA containing two primary coding regions – rep and cap – flanked by inverted-terminal repeats (ITR)[10]. The rep region encodes four essential proteins that play pivotal roles in viral replication and genome encapsidation. Furthermore, the cap region encodes three viral capsid proteins, VP1, VP2 and VP3, which assemble into T=1 icosahedral capsid. In addition, alternate reading frames in cap encode the assembly-activation protein (AAP)[11], membrane-associated accessory protein (MAAP)[12,13], and X protein[14].

The deterministic factor of AAV tropism is the capsid proteins. Comparative analysis of sequences and structures across AAV serotypes readily identifies non-conserved, surface-exposed capsid regions, and modifications in these areas can significantly alter AAV’s interaction with host tissues and cellular receptors, motivating efforts to engineer AAV tropism[15]. An increasing number of approaches have been employed to introduce and screen for diversity across the capsid to enable directed evolution, with a focus on the non-conserved regions. These methods for generating libraries include error prone PCR[16,17], capsid shuffling[18–20], variable regions (VR) virtual shuffling[21], “loop swap”[22], and peptide display[23].

Briefly, error prone PCR introduces random mutations across cap, including regions that can potentially influence both the binding and trafficking of the resulting virus[16,17]. A capsid shuffled library is generated by primerless PCR assembly of fragmented cap DNA sequences from multiple AAV serotypes. The resulting chimeric capsids combinatorically inherit different variable regions from multiple serotypes, altering and potentially enhancing their efficacy and/or specificity[18–20]. A VR shuffling library is generated through identifying VR lineages and synthesizing the fragments through degenerate homoduplex recombination and constructing the final library by combining compatible regions[21]. “Loop swap” libraries were constructed through identifying AAV capsid surface “loop” regions that are critical for viral transduction, then replacing them with semi-random sequences determined by bioinformatical analysis of cap genes from GenBank database[22]. Finally, peptide display libraries involve inserting peptides of varying length into the three-fold protrusion, which enables the acquisition of new receptor interaction function while simultaneously compromising the capsid’s intrinsic cell tropism[24] (Figure 1).

Libraries are then exposed to selective pressures for enhanced fitness. The first criterion is viability packaging efficiency, where production of variant AAV capsids, encoded by their variant cap genes, selects for virions that can assemble and package a genome. This stage is critical for the success of library generation and overall library diversity. An additional early property that has been investigated, initially in vitro, was the evasion of neutralizing antibodies to potentially enhance their therapeutic efficacy in patients previously exposed to natural AAVs[25]. Another important property is cell-type tropism or selectivity, i.e., selection for AAV variants for enhanced localization to an intended cell populations and/or reduced off-target biodistribution, though specificity has been challenging as it is difficult to experimentally select for the lack of localization to an off-target region. Finally, enhanced infectivity – the capacity for enhanced cellular uptake and efficient nuclear localization[26–31], uncoating[32], and gene expression– is sometimes included in a selection[33] (Figure 2). Upon subjecting AAV libraries to rigorous selection to direct their evolution, fit variants are recovered and subjected to analysis and/or additional rounds of rescreening. Over time, superior variants begin to dominate the pool – in a manner emulating natural evolution – to result in a new generation of AAVs with enhanced phenotypes (Figure 1).

## Computationally Guided AAV Capsid Designs

The first step for the directed evolution is creating a genetically diversified AAV library, and a range of approaches have been developed as discussed above. One challenge is that, given the inherently random nature by which diversity is typically introduced into libraries, a considerable proportion of the library is potentially nonviable due to factors such as nonsense mutations, structural instability, or suboptimal packaging efficiency[9,34]. Due to the resource-intensive nature of library selection, it would be ideal to maximize the quality of the input libraries. Bioinformatic and computational approaches have increasingly played a role in library design. One early such effort was “loop swap” libraries, which as described above involved semi-randomization of hypervariable loops guided by natural AAV sequence alignment[22]. However, computation has been playing an increasingly important role in capsid library engineering, as we discuss below.

### Rationally Driven Computational Capsid Design

#### SCHEMA Libraries

In vitro recombination techniques such as DNA shuffling are powerful tools for protein evolution[35]. In the early 2000s, the Arnold group recognized that placing domains from disparate protein parents into the same structure could be structurally destabilizing and developed the computational algorithm SCHEMA, which identifies the recombination crossover positions within two parental proteins that minimize structural disruption within the resulting chimeric progeny[36]. This technique can be further used to predict functional chimera sequences[36,37].

In 2013, Ho et al. applied a SCHEMA algorithm to AAVs by recombining AAV serotypes 2 and 4 to create 17 new chimeric capsids containing a single crossover position, and they evaluated the resulting capsid assembly and cellular transduction[38]. Interestingly, they didn’t observe a clear correlation between the predicted, calculated structure disruption and viral assembly or transduction, which may have been due to the small library size that was investigated.

Ojala et al. applied SCHEMA to create an AAV library with millions of variants. In particular, they identified 7 crossover positions that both minimized predicted structural disruption and shuffled key structural features of capsids, such as surface loops and hypervariable regions, while ensuring a relatively more even distribution of the block sizes. They then recombined the cap genes of 6 clinically relevant serotypes (AAV2, 4, 5, 6, 8 and 9) at these positions using golden gate cloning[39]. Selective pressure was applied to identify optimal variants for specific applications (Figure 3), in this case the capacity to infect a specific neural stem cell population in the adult mouse brain. The result was a novel variant that mediated 24-fold higher GFP expression and greater transduction volume compared to AAV9 in adult neural stem cells in the subventricular zone[39]. These studies further established the potential of rational, computational strategies for AAV library design.

#### Ancestral Libraries

Another example of rational, computationally aided library design was the generation of ancestral AAV libraries, as illustrated by studies from Santiago-Ortiz et al. and Zinn et al.[40,41]. Ancestral reconstruction involves the phylogenetic analysis of current, natural biomolecular variant sequences to enable computational prediction of putative ancestors. Given that ancestral variants gave rise to extant AAVs, they are by definition evolvable and can serve as a “plastic” starting template for further engineering.

Santiago-Ortiz et al. and Zinn et al., employed different computational algorithms and approaches for ancestral reconstruction. Santiago-Ortiz et al. employed Markov chain Monte Carlo-based simulation of the phylogenetic tree space, with particular focus on predicting with high confidence an ancestral node for AAV1, 6, 7, and other existing variants[41]. For this node, all capsid amino acid positions except 32 could be predicted with a >0.9 confidence, and at these 32 positions, for which 2 or 3 possible amino acid identities were predicted with high confidence. A library in which the experimental amino acid frequencies matched the computationally predicted amino acid probabilities at these 32 positions was designed and synthesized, resulting in a pool with a theoretical diversity of 2.5x1011. Following six sequential rounds of directed evolution in C2C12 mouse myoblast cells, the resulting variants not only demonstrated increased thermostability and increased in vivo transgene expression relative to AAV1, but also exhibited altered cell receptor usage. These results underscore the potential for deriving not only new AAVs but also new mechanistic insights into AAV-host interactions from ancestral reconstruction[41].

In contrast, Zinn et al. employed an ancestral sequence reconstruction based on an empirical likelihood model, identifying a node that included most AAV serotypes except AAV4 and 5[40]. The approach identified 11 variable amino acid positions, each with 2 possible amino acid identities, resulting in an ancestral library with 2048 distinct variants. The initial screening of 776 individual variants using in vitro assays highlighted the Anc80L65 variant, which also exhibited superior thermostability. Further analysis demonstrated Anc80L65’s ability to transduce photoreceptors, liver, muscle, and inner hair cells in mouse as well as liver cells in non-human primate[42]. A subsequent study performed by the same group introduced unique barcodes into each of 2048 ancestral library variants to permit high throughput screening with NGS platforms[43]. Multiparametric screening using in vitro and in vivo mouse and non-human primate models led to the discovery that a single G-to-A residue mutation at amino acid position 266 could modulate the liver tropism of the ancestral capsids[42]. This was found to be functionally conserved in AAV9 and AAV3B serotypes, further emphasizing the strong potential of using ancestral library constructions as an engineering approach to generate novel AAV capsids with enhanced functionalities and potentially unravel hidden traits acquired during nature’s evolution.

### Machine Learning Based Capsid Discovery

#### Next-Generation Sequencing of AAV Libraries.

The advent of Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS) has enabled data-guided AAV engineering. Currently, Illumina benchtop sequencers can generate 4 million to 1.5 billion reads per run with a read length of 2x150-300 bp, whereas a production-scale sequencer can generate 1.2 billion to 52 billion reads per run primarily with a 2x150 bp read length, enabling an unparalleled depth of library analysis[44]. Given the short 150-300 bp read length, Illumina NGS is ideally suited for the analysis of libraries that feature single peptide insertions[1,45], although new computational methods are being developed to seamlessly handle reads that are shorter than the window of diversity being engineered[45]. Such a method could be used, for example, on libraries in which variation spans the entire cap sequence while individual NGS amplicon reads cannot capture the entire cap gene. Other strategies could involve generating small blocks of cap gene linked with a unique barcode. The cap gene library can then be constructed by sequentially piece together the cap fragments while placing the corresponding barcode outside of the coding region. Sequencing the resulting barcode combination would reveal the identity of cap variants[43]. Alternatively, long-read sequencing technologies such as Pacific Bioscience (PacBio) and Oxford Nanopore are readily capable of fully sequencing cap. While the current read count of ~1-10 million per run for these technologies is lower than Illumina, and the error rate is higher, progress in sequencing depth and accuracy is increasingly making these tools useful[44]. Several studies have successfully leveraged long-read sequencing technologies to assess both the integrity and heterogeneity of packaged AAV transgenes[46–48], highlighting the feasibility and potential of applying these technologies for AAV library analysis. Additionally, the computational modeling strategy mentioned earlier[45]—to handle reads that don’t span the full window being engineered—, can also help overcome issues rising from low read counts. The underlying statistical mechanism enabling these advances is the ability to automatically deduce how to appropriately share information across distinct reads, by way of machine learning.

#### Machine Learning Applications.

Machine learning (ML), or as it’s now often called, artificial intelligence (AI), has been increasingly harnessed in AAV engineering[49,50]. ML focuses on automatically identifying important patterns found in training data, so that the patterns can be inspected to glean scientific hypotheses, or, be leveraged to test/design future data[51]. Within AAV engineering, ML has been used to build predictive models for AAV properties such as viability and/or delivery, from sequence, and then to leverage these models to design capsid libraries, or individual capsids, with enhanced versions of these properties (Figure 4). In designing a library, one must balance diversity, with the predicted value of the desired property[34,52].

ML methods can be broadly categorized as supervised or unsupervised. No matter which category an ML method falls into, a user will have to contend with numerical optimization to find parameters, and likely also uncertainty quantification on the predictions and/or parameters, and elements of decision theory[51]. Supervised models, those most-used for AAV capsid engineering, are trained on sets of paired data, where each element of the set comprises an input, such as a capsid sequence, and paired with it, a supervisory label, such as a packaging efficiency readout. The idea is to learn a mapping from the input sequence to the prediction label, from the training data, in a manner that works on sequences not observed during training. The mapping is “learned” by comparing predictions of the model to their actual value, and adjusting the parameters of the model in a direction that closes the gap. This process is performed automatically using techniques from numerical optimization. To assess how well one might perform on future, unseen data, we partition the data we have, and pretend that for some portion of it that we haven’t observed the labels, removing these from the training data, so that they are not used to estimate the model parameters. Then we train our model using the training data, and then use the model to predict the labels of those data we “held out” of the training procedure. We can then compare the predictions with the actual labels, reporting, for example, the mean squared error between them, or a correlation (Figure 4). If the test data comes from the same distribution as the training data, and both are sufficiently large, then such an assessment can prove useful. To instantiate these ideas within the context of AAV, variant sequences can be “labeled” with log enrichment scores[34,45], which quantifies the relative extent to which each variant passes a selection, such as for capsid assembly and incorporation of a genome, i.e., viral viability[34,50]. In addition to viral viability, supervised models have been used to study properties of the AAV capsids such as antibody neutralization[53] and cellular transduction[54–56] (Figure 4).

Unsupervised models focus on pattern recognition within unlabeled data, meaning those without a paired supervisory label[57]. Instantiations include clustering, where the model groups the input data into clusters based on data similarities, as well as dimensionality reduction for visualization and representation extraction[51]. Several AAV studies have used unsupervised approaches for capsid diversification to discover new variants[58,59]. For example, Sinai et al. focused on a 28-amino-acid segment (capsid positions 560-588) in the AAV2 VP1[59], training a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) on a Multiple Sequence Alignment (MSA) of dependo-parvoviruses data[51] Notably, even though we may term such an approach unsupervised, curating an MSA data set to train such a model—based, say on a wild type seed sequence—is implicitly injecting a “soft” label in the sense that each sequence in the MSA is thought to be evolutionarily-related to the seed sequence. Consequently, such a modeling approach is sometimes referred to as “weak-positive semi-supervised learning”[60]. In the case of Sinai et al, they additionally augmented the MSA data with sequences deemed to be viable by way of a mutational scan, comprising variants up to 23 substitutions away from the wild type. The approach was adapted from Bryant et al.[49]. This brings us to our next topic of semi-supervised learning.

In addition to supervised and unsupervised models, one can also use semi-supervised models, which make use of both labeled and unlabeled data[57]. Huang et al. developed a Supervised Variational Auto-encoder (SVAE) model with the goal of improving AAV capsid targeting of the CNS via binding to specific host cell proteins. In particular, they focused on two host cell proteins, LY6A and LY6C1, expressed on the murine blood-brain barrier (BBB)[53]. They found that a single round of in vitro binding assay, performed by incubating an AAV library with protein-presenting beads and selecting for bound variants, yielded variants with enhanced mice CNS transduction. The resulting data were used to generate more diverse and selective variants[53]. This approach led to variants exhibiting significantly higher gene expression in mouse brain when administered intravenously, highlighting the potential benefits of combining in vitro and in silico models for effective variants design.

Upon deciding on a particular modeling strategy, such as a supervised approach, and having the data in hand, one typically compares the performance of several different models, assessing which is best on a held-out test set as described earlier. For example, Marques et al. created an AAV2 capsid library by diversifying a 33 amino acid residues, which was identified through in vivo directed evolution of the VR shuffling library[21]. The mutations were introduced using degenerate primers (e.g., NVN, DSN) to obtain viral viability-labeled data. They then trained two classes of models, neural networks, and several Support Vector Machines (SVM), each with a kernel[50]; in neural networks, this type of “inductive bias” is instead determined by the architecture of the network, such as the number of hidden layers. Marques et al. found that the neural network achieved higher predictive accuracy than the SVM. As it is impossible to compare all SVMs to all neural networks, the generality of such statements should be taken with a grain of salt. In addition to trying different model classes, different sequence representations can also be used, such as “one hot” encoding, wherein each position is encoded as a binary vector of length 20 (for 20 amino acids), with only one bit “on” (all elements of the vector are set to 0 other than the bit that refers to that amino acid). One can instead/also use a representation based on amino acid physiochemical properties or from an ML-learned representation, such as from evolutionary scale modeling (ESM-1b)[61].

Using a model referred to as an LSTM, Eid et al. developed a AAV9-7mer library and investigated multiple AAV functions including viability, cell transduction, and liver targeting through packaging, in vivo screening, and in vitro screening[55]. The top predicted liver targeting capsids exhibited high viral productivity, murine liver transduction, and significantly enhanced human hepatocyte transduction (1000-fold increase compared to AAV9, though AAV9 is not necessarily highly efficient on hepatocytes in vitro). Importantly, the top predicted variants from mice tissue and human cell culture also mediated high transduction efficiency in macaque liver, revealing the potential of using machine learning model for cross-species predictions[55].

Bryant et al. explored not only what supervised model classes worked well for their AAV problem, but also how different training data sampling strategies affect the predictive accuracy of a binary classification model for viability[49]. For example, they consider using data with only 2 mutations, or 2-10 mutations, using randomly chosen sequences versus those chosen with the help of a ML model, etc. They focused on a 28 amino-acid segment, and explored three model classes: logistic regression, convolutional neural network (CNN), and recurrent neural network (RNN) models. Logistic regression is a simple, but often effective baseline model, while RNNs and CNNs can capture more complex sequence epistasis given only simple sequence features. The study found that CNNs and RNNs outperformed logistic regression models in predicting viable AAV capsid designs.

Although most AAV viability studies to date have focused on AAV2, Zhu et al. explored predicting the viability of AAV5-7mer variants, and then designing diverse libraries comprising generally viable variants[34]. Three linear additive models and four neural network models were investigated, with neural network models slightly outperforming the other models. Having trained the model, the authors developed a computational library design method to leverage this model to trace out a set of libraries that navigate the diversity-viability optimal frontier. They then choose several of these ML-designed libraries to construct and test in the lab. Ultimately, they find that a ML-designed library yielded superior assembly and high efficiency transduction of primary human brain tissue slices[34]. Consequently, the authors succeeded in demonstrating how to design a broadly useful library—one that is diverse and contains viable sequences—for potentially any downstream selection task.

## Computational Approaches for AAV Regulatory Elements

While capsid diversification techniques have enhanced AAV infectivity and targeting, complementary advances in the engineering of genetic payloads are augmenting both the expression potency and specificity of AAV cargoes, specifically through the incorporation of cell- and tissue-specific gene regulatory elements such as promoters and enhancers (Figure 5). To accommodate the limited genetic payload size of AAV, such regulatory elements must be small yet still potent. Efforts to identify and utilize such elements have concentrated on two fronts: the exploration of endogenous enhancers and the creation of synthetic promoters[62]

Eukaryotic promoters primarily consist of two elements, a core and a proximal region. The core region serves as the minimal DNA sequence required to initiate RNA polymerase II transcription, and the upstream proximal promoter region tunes gene expression levels. Since transcription factor activity can be cell type-specific[63], proximal promoter regions – which consist of a series of transcription factor binding sites – are largely the focus in engineered promoter design.

To identify natural regulatory elements, regions of the genome are analyzed for expression, chromatin accessibility, histone modifications, and/or transcription factor binding capacity—typically using techniques such as ATAC-seq, ChIP-seq, and single-cell transcriptomics data[64]. These comprehensive datasets can then be leveraged by predictive computational models to enhance promoter identification in DNA sequences of interest. Tools like iProEP utilize a SVM to distinguish a promoter from a non-promoter in five separate species[65]. Additionally, deep learning models such as DeePromotery[66], Nvwa[67], and Enformer[68] have been effective in predicting novel regulatory elements. Another model, STARR-seq, utilizes the episomal and chromatin-free status of the AAV genome to elucidate previously undetected enhancer elements. The technique was recently utilized to generate and screen in vivo an impressively massive library spanning 3 Mb (~0.1%) of the mouse genome[69], and the pipeline uses a computational framework called STARRPeaker to identify enhancers[70].

The mere identification of a regulatory element does not guarantee its utility in gene therapies, however. Most natural regulatory elements are too large to package into AAV, and truncation of large endogenous elements can compromise their function. Thus, the generation and subsequent screening of large, synthetic promoter libraries offers a desirable alternative, as synthetic promoter constructs have the ability to preserve cell-specificity with tunable strength and length. Several library types have been generated, including combinatorial addition of key natural promoter regions, targeted mutagenesis of existing promoters, and oligomerization of transcription factor binding sites[62]. Despite their potential, the use of promoter libraries in AAV has so far been sparse, with one notable example in which a 230-element synthetic promoter library was screened to successfully identify cell- and species-specific AAV constructs[71].

Once a natural or synthetic promoter library is constructed, it can be screened for the desired function, such as strength or cell-specificity. In the case of AAV-based promoter engineering, the library is packaged into an AAV capsid. Upon infecting cells or organisms of interest, individual promoter strengths are evaluated by the expression of a fluorescent reporter protein, generally through fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) or RNA-seq[72]. Individual promoter identity may be conferred through FACS-mediated binning or by a unique, transcribed barcode, and NGS is then conducted to identify top variants. Notably, the STARR-seq approach eliminated the need for barcoding by generating self-transcribing enhancer elements 3’ of a core promoter[69]. Promoters can also be screened for cell-state specificity (Figure 5). For example, by creating a synthetic promoter library wherein each construct consists of tandem repeats of a single transcription factor binding site, a pipeline called SPECS identified promoters that drive expression in cancerous cells but not in healthy cells[73]. To reduce cost and labor, the use of computational methods to better inform the promoter screening process is on the rise: for instance, computational frameworks such as neural networks can be used to screen larger promoter libraries, predict promoter expression strength[74], or identify sequences within promoters most responsible for high expression[75].

Despite advances in regulatory element detection and screening, applying these computationally guided frameworks to AAV genome engineering for more efficient and cell type-specific transgenic expression is still at an early stage. However, we anticipate promoter engineering to play a crucial future role in gene therapy and the treatment of human disease.

## Concluding remarks

While medicine has made tremendous progress over the past few decades, many prevalent diseases still have no effective treatment. AAV-based gene therapies offer considerable potential for addressing these medical needs, though to date challenges with efficacy, cost, and to an extent safety have challenged progress in the field. Computational approaches offer great potential and guidance in the design of novel AAV libraries that lead to superior AAV variants with high efficiency, targeted delivery, a correspondingly decreased dosage, and likewise lower cost and potentially higher safety (see Outstanding questions). Moreover, with rapid progress in NGS technologies, big data emerging from AAV library generation and selection studies are being leveraged with machine learning to enable new basic virology insights and new AAV variants with enhanced properties, further showcasing the power of data-driven strategies in biological research and design.

## Abstract

Seizures are made up of the coordinated activity of networks of neurons, suggesting that control of neurons in the pathologic circuits of epilepsy could allow for control of the disease. Optogenetics has been effective at stopping seizure-like activity in non-human disease models by increasing inhibitory tone or decreasing excitation, though this effect has not been shown in human brain tissue. Many of the genetic means for achieving channelrhodopsin expression in non-human models are not possible in humans, and vector-mediated methods are susceptible to species-specific tropism that may affect translational potential. Here, we demonstrate AAV-mediated, optogenetic reductions in network firing rates of human hippocampal slices recorded on high-density microelectrode arrays under several hyperactivity provoking conditions. This platform can serve to bridge the gap between human and animal studies by exploring genetic interventions on network activity human brain tissue.

## INTRODUCTION

Epilepsy is a disease of aberrant neuronal activity that results from an imbalance of excitation and inhibition1–3. Francis Crick famously envisioned the potential of using light to precisely control neuronal populations in the human brain4–6. Since their discovery, light-responsive channelrhodopsins7 have become a cornerstone of modern neuroscience studies8,9. While optogenetic interventions have shown tremendous promise in non-human disease models of epilepsy10,11, whether such tools will translate into human neural circuits, and under what conditions, remains unclear.

Although direct application of optogenetics in the human brain is not currently possible, it has been translated for use in human retina12,13. The use of optogenetics in research on human brain tissue has the potential to uncover key parameters for evaluating the potential efficacy of alternative therapeutic strategies. Development of any such therapies involving vector delivery of activity modulating genes would benefit from data in a directly relevant model, namely human brain tissue.

Human brain tissue slices have been used to probe mechanisms of epilepsy for decades14–17, and single neuron patch clamping data exists showing cells transduced with an activating channelrhodopsin in human brain slice can be depolarized with light18. However, optogenetics has never been used to modulate network activity in a human brain slice model. Activation of inhibitory GABAergic neurons10,19 and silencing of glutamatergic neurons20,21 have both shown promise in animal models of epilepsy. Still, neither of these approaches have been demonstrated in human brain slice.

Despite meaningful insights into human hippocampal physiology, the vectors, genetic models and optogenetic techniques available for circuit manipulation in non-human models have far outpaced those developed for human brain slice models21–26. Species-specific differences present a significant barrier to developing therapeutic modalities27,28 since cross-species applicability can be unpredictable. A model for evaluating AAVs in human brain slice models of human disease may provide a valuable method to screen for translational potential.

Tools for delivering genetic payloads to specific neuronal cell types in a model-agnostic way are advancing rapidly29–33, and offer therapeutic potential32,34,35. For example, if AAV vectors can be combined with enhancers or promoters that selectively promote gene expression in a molecularly defined subset of cells, this would allow investigation of how optogenetic control of specific cell types could impact network activity, providing a roadmap to developing interventions that modulate epileptiform activity22,36–38.

Here, we seek to validate a platform that addresses the unmet need to evaluate optogenetic interventions on network activity in human brain tissue. To this end, we evaluate the network effects of AAV-mediated optogenetic activity modulation in a human brain slice model of epileptiform activity. From the view of epilepsy as an imbalance of excitation and inhibition1, we choose to target excitability in excitatory neurons. We hypothesized that inhibition of a subset of glutamatergic cells can limit epileptiform activity in human hippocampal network.

## RESULTS

### Human hippocampus slice culture and neuronal transduction

To model human epileptiform activity, we established human organotypic tissue slices from hippocampus tissue (Fig.1a) donated to research by patients with drug-refractory epilepsy. Tissues were obtained from patients both with and without hippocampal sclerosis as defined by ILAE criteria39 (Table 1). Resected tissue was sliced to 300µm and cultured on cell inserts at the air-liquid interface in serum-free media as previously described16,36. Slices were transduced (see Methods) with AAV9 carrying a HcKCR140 transgene driven by a CAMK2A promoter and a fluorescent tag (eYFP). Fluorescent reporter expression was observed in live imaging with an epi-fluorescent microscope by day 4–6 (transduced on day 0). On the day of experiments, the slice is plated with neuron-dense areas of interest positioned over the HD-MEA recording surface (Fig. 1b). A scan of the recording area electrodes is performed immediately after plating the slice to observe areas of spontaneous activity (Fig. 1c). After experiments, slices are fixed and reporter expression is confirmed by immunohistochemistry (Fig. 1d & Extended Data Fig. 1). Reporter expression was enriched in neurons of the granule cell layer and the dentate gyrus as well as pyramidal cells (Fig. 1e, Extended data Fig. 1). The proportion of neurons expressing eYFP in areas of high transduction ranged from 10 – 54% (Table 2). This variability may be the result of focal micropipette injection. Slices that did not show detectable eYFP were excluded from the analysis of transduction rates (see methods). Together, these results indicate that we established organotypic tissue slice cultures of the human hippocampus and reproducibly deliver genetic payloads into hippocampal glutamatergic neurons using a combination of AAV9 and CAMK2A promoter driven transcript.

### Optogenetic control of human hippocampal network

HcKCR1 encodes a kalium channelrhodopsin, a potassium-selective, light-sensitive ion channel that hyperpolarizes the neuronal membrane, thus reducing the probability of spiking when activated by 530nm light40,41. Unlike a more traditional Channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2), which encodes a sodium selective ion channel, inhibitory channelrhodopsin has never been applied to human tissue. To confirm that HcKCR1 illumination drives membrane hyperpolarization, we conducted intracellular voltage clamp recordings. Consistent with our expectations, HcKCR1 activation results in hyperpolarizing currents in human hippocampal neurons (Extended Data Fig. 2). To assess whether AAV-based transduction of human neurons with optogenetic constructs is specific to HcKCR1, we transduced additional slices with an excitatory channelrhodopsin (AAV9-CAMK2A-ChR2-eYFP) packaged in the same viral vector. In this case, we observed similar extent of expression, suggesting that our methods are not limited to HcKCR1 (Extended Data Fig. 1). Together, these results demonstrate the feasibility of applying inhibitory optogenetics to human neurons.

### Computational modeling of glutamatergic neuron inhibition

Relative rarity of human hippocampal tissue samples and the limited viability of slices can impede optimization of any step in an experimental protocol that direct testing of human tissue. Computational modeling of cellular circuits is free from these limitations. We conducted in silico modeling of hippocampal epileptiform activity based on prior electrophysiological data42 to computationally predict the degree to which HcKCR1 activation might dampen epileptiform activity across a range of transduction rates in human neurons,. The model contains dentate gyrus granule cells providing excitatory input and basket cells providing inhibitory input. In the model, the light-sensitive channel is modelled after the single cell characterization of HcKCR140. We varied the proportion of granule cells expressing this channel to model the potential effects of variability in expression levels (Extended data Fig. 3). In silico epileptiform activity could be dampened with optogenetic control of less than 50% of the granule cell population (Extended data Fig. 3). Even at the lower limits of effective expression, the length and intensity of seizure-like events are experimentally controllable in our model (Extended Data Fig. 3). This analysis suggests that even incomplete delivery of HcKCR1 into glutamatergic hippocampal neurons may be sufficient to modulate network-level epileptiform activity.

### HD-MEA integration with optogenetic activation

To test the effects of optically activating channelrhodopsins in our slice model, we integrated the HD-MEA recording system with fiber-coupled LED drivers to illuminate organotypic slices plated on the recording array. The associated hardware is small enough to contained entirely in a tissue culture incubator (Fig. 2, Supplemental Fig. S1, Supplemental Table ST1). While closed in the incubator, the system is controllable from external computers. Custom software was created to allow for real-time analysis of spike event data, allowing for observation of electrophysiological activity and the impact of optogenetic perturbations with minimal delay. The system allows software control of light intensity, duration, frequency, and off-time.

### Optical HcKCR1-mediated inhibition of network activity

HcKCR1 activation suppressed activity in human hippocampal neurons across all experimental conditions of spontaneous and provoked activity (Fig. 3, Table 2). Illumination with 530nm light40 resulted in rapid silencing of hippocampal activity (Fig. 3, Extended Data Fig. 4 - 6). Constant illumination for 10 seconds reduces spontaneous firing rates (Fig. 3a). Changes in spike amplitude were less consistent (Extended Data Fig. 4, Supplemental Table ST2). The reduction in neuronal spiking was consistent and evident in raw data (Fig. 3a, Video 1, Extended Data Fig. 4, Supplemental Table ST2).

Intensity scans across the full range of light intensity produced by the LED driver were carried out to determine the dynamic range of the control of neuronal firing rates as a function of illumination power (Extended Data Fig. 7). The intensity threshold was typically between (26.2 mW/mm2 - 31.2 mW/mm2), correlating to 40–50% of the possible output from our drivers. For experiments, we utilized one step above the minimum threshold (i.e., 50 – 60% intensity, translating to 31.2 – 35.8 mW/mm2).

Decreases in neuronal firing rates during HcKCR1 optogenetic activation were obtained from n=8 ex vivo hippocampal slices (Table 2, Extended Data Fig. 4-6). We additionally carried out recordings in a hippocampal slice transduced with an identical AAV vector driving ChR2 expression (AAV9-CAMK2A-ChR2-eYFP), which demonstrated an increase in unit activity with 470nm light illumination (Extended Data Fig. 8). This result confirms the specificity of light-mediated change in neuronal activity is determined by the channelrhodopsin-specific physiology and not an artifact of light illumination.

AAV-mediated of HcKCR1 is sufficient to enable optogenetic modulation of network-wide spontaneous activity despite incomplete transduction (Table 2). Spontaneous activity arises from networks perched in a balanced regime that is neither prone to silence nor saturation43. As a result, relatively small increases in inhibitory tone at a cellular level may be insufficient to offset the imbalance necessary to generate epileptiform activity at a network level.

### Optogenetic suppression in provoked hyperexcitability

Next, we tested HcKCR1-mediated optical inhibition in the context of hyperexcitable conditions. Under all these conditions, HcKCR1 activation reduced firing rates in large portions of units recorded (Table 2).

We used a magnesium-free (0-mg) media, a long-standing approach used to increase neuronal excitability and induce epileptiform activity in hippocampal preparations14,44,45. Clear, spontaneous bursts of activity were observed 2/4 slices bathed with 0-mg media (Fig. 3c, Extended data Fig. 5 & 9, Supplemental Table ST3). These bursts of activity were <1s in duration and several minutes apart, reminiscent of interictal epileptiform spikes46. During LED light illumination of slices bathed in 0-mg media, mean firing rates were reduced compared to the rates in the absence of light illumination, although not all units responded uniformly. As an example of this spectrum of unit response, average firing rate reduction of the grouped unit activity in two slices did not meet statistical significance in the zero-magnesium media conditions (Extended Data Fig. 5, Supplemental Table ST3). On a unit-level analysis, however (and evident in raster plots of Extended Data Fig. 5g & j), 15 – 40% of units in these slices had a decrease in firing rate of at least 90% during light-ON conditions (Table 2, 11G & 12G), demonstrating that not all units in each slice respond uniformly .Spike events during 0-mg recording conditions were not completely absent during optical inhibition two separate slices (Fig. 3 c, t10, Extended data Fig. 5 d & g). The spikes were far enough apart in time to prevent strong conclusions about the effects of optical inhibition on these events (Extended data Fig. 9).

Addition of kainic acid (KA) has been used in various epilepsy models22,47–49. Based on other groups reporting the effectiveness of combining multiple pro-convulsant pharmacologic interventions to induce epileptiform activity22,50, we tested whether adding kainate to 0-mg bathed slices would lead to epileptiform activity. The addition of KA resulted in acute elevations in firing rate, and in 2/4 slices recorded with KA, rhythmic bursts of activity occurred (Fig. 3d, Extended Data Fig. 6 d & g). Slices exhibiting this rhythmic bursting of unit activity also showed increased coherence across most frequency power bands, most clearly in the theta band (Fig. 3 f-g). Repeated 10s periods of illumination reduced firing rates during light-ON conditions (Fig. 3d), but a causal effect of illumination on the coordinated bursts is less clear in the absence of more comprehensive characterization of the typical effects and expected frequency of rhythmic bursting with addition of KA (Extended Data Fig. 6, Supplemental Table ST4).

To explore this platform’s ability to perform closed-loop illumination, we used a GABAAR blockade via the application of bicuculline to elevate firing rates above their baseline levels (Fig. 3 j-k). We utilized the reproducible increases in firing rate with GABAAR blockade to detect and disrupt elevations in network firing. We use an automated, real-time spike event detection to trigger LED illumination when a firing rate threshold. (Fig. 3h-k). The closed-loop illumination software activates following bicuculline application, and firing rates surpassing the threshold triggers 10-seconds of continuous illumination. This dramatically reduced the firing of recorded units (Fig.3h-k, Video 2). This was replicated in n=3 HcKCR1-expressing slices derived from n=2 patients. These results demonstrate a potential benefit of optogenetic interventions in epilepsy: modulation of brain activity restricted precisely to time and anatomy in which pathologic elevations in neuronal firing occur.

In these three distinct methods of provoking a hyperexcitable state (0-mg, 0-mg+KA and GABAAR blockade), HcKCR1 activation in a subset of glutamatergic CAMK2A-expressing neurons reduced network firing rates. Fraction of neurons transduced in a recording area did not completely explain different fractions of neurons exhibiting reduced firing rates in light-ON conditions (Table 2, Supplemental Fig. S2). The magnitude of firing rate reductions in 0-mg and 0-mg+KA conditions was less than that observed in physiologic media and GABAergic blockade (Supplemental Fig S3). While several variables may contribute to this, HcKCR1-mediated inhibition of presynaptic CAMK2A-expressing neurons may be partially offset by post-synaptic glutamatergic receptor activation in 0-mg and 0-mg+KA conditions. Whether HcKCR1 activation of CAMK2A-expressing neurons effectively interrupt provoked coherence seen in 0-mg + KA conditions will require additional experiments to thoroughly characterize the effects of the rhythmic burst activity induced with 0-mg + KA.

### Propagation of epileptiform activity

Spatially resolved recordings of neural activity enabled by the HD-MEA allow us to analyze signal propagation patterns over the hippocampal areas recorded during epileptiform spikes and optogenetic activation of HcKCR1. First, we examined increases in single unit firing rates during the 0-mg+KA spike events that make up the rhythmic bursting in the slice with the densest coverage of the GCL. Plotting the units with relative increases of >3 standard deviations above their baseline firing before the spike event suggested a progression from the hilar aspect of the GCL to the outer aspect (Fig. 4 a-c). Due to the theta phase coherence observed at a network level during these bursts of activity (Fig. 3 f - h), we examined the spatial changes in phase coherence over time during these rhythmic bursts. Plotting the relative change in the theta phase during these bursts of activity reveals clear propagation of theta waves from the hilar aspect to the outer aspect of the GCL (Fig. 4 d, Video 3). A comparable pattern of theta propagation was also observed in the rhythmic bursting during 0-mg+KA in a separate slice, also with GCL coverage, from a different patient (Video 4).

In one slice there was no overlap of these rhythmic bursts during light-ON conditions (Extended Data Fig. 6 g), while in the other slice these bursts did indeed have some overlap with the light-ON conditions (Fig 3 d, t6-t8). This variability suggests that reductions in overall firing rate, or reductions in CAMK2A+ neuronal firing, may not always be sufficient for disrupting network coherence characteristic of epileptic circuits.

The traveling wave phenotype we observed has never been visualized at this level of resolution. Such a granular picture of network synchronization may offer a proxy for epileptiform activity that has been unmeasurable without HD-MEA technology. These traveling waves of theta coherence during 0-mg+KA may offer targets for evaluating the efficacy of experimental interventions.

### Waveform and opto-response clustering

Reduced unit firing with HcKCR1 activation was not uniform across recorded units (Fig. 3, Extended Data Figure 4 - 6), ranging from complete silencing to more subtle or no apparent firing rate changes in other units. Given that AAV9 transduction was not uniform across the tissue, this may partially explain such a spectrum of response, but there was not a clear correlation between transduction rate and fractions of units with reduced firing (Supplemental Fig. S2). However, cell type is another variable that could affect a unit’s response to HcKCR1 activation even in the presence of similar transduction. To investigate whether response parameters of the units are uniform40,51, we investigated whether unit cell-type differences could be inferred from the HD-MEA extracellular recordings.

We applied a waveform clustering method52,53 (see Extended Data Methods) to group units based on features extracted from the extracellular action-potential waveform (Fig. 5). This analysis yielded 12 separate clusters (Fig. 5). To validate whether the distribution of putative cell types identified by waveform clustering is consistent with anatomy, we aligned recording array electrodes with histology to approximate the anatomic slice area from which each electrode is records. If waveform clusters correlate with putative cell types, then recordings over an anatomic area with a relatively homogenous cell type should be enriched for waveform clusters underrepresented in anatomic areas without such cells. We analyzed waveform clustering in areas of the dentate gyrus granule cell layer (GCL) versus recordings without granule cell layer representation. We compared the distribution of unit waveform cluster in 3 slices with clear GCL coverage to 6 slices recorded where active recording electrodes did not overlap with GCL. Five waveform clusters were significantly overrepresented in the GCL recordings (Fig. 5, Supplemental Table ST5).

Next, to characterize the heterogeneity of unit responses to optogenetic activation, we used an HDBSCAN-based clustering technique54,55 (see Extended Data Methods). We analyzed peri-stimulus histograms of neuronal firing rate spanning time segments before and during optogenetic activation. We found 5 distinct opto-response clusters (Fig. 6 a, b), 4 of which showed statistically significant reductions in mean firing rate and firing rate distribution with optogenetic activation (Fig. 6 c).

Since our waveform clustering suggested that 5 of the waveform clusters were associated with recordings of the GCL, we treated these waveform clusters as a single category when testing whether opto-response clusters were associated with any putative cell types from waveform clustering. There was indeed a significant association between the GCL waveform cluster and the opto-response cluster 3 (Supplemental Table ST6), in addition to associations between several other waveform and opto-response clusters. While this is far from definitive for stipulating cell type to be the only or most prominent factor in neuronal response to HcKCR1 activation, it is consistent with the hypothesis that response to optogenetic activation may differ between cell types. Moreover, it suggests the need for further clarification of how optogenetic interventions in different cell-types may affect those cell-types and networks differently.

## DISCUSSION

We describe an approach for using human organotypic brain tissue as an experimental research platform for optimizing approaches to modulate neural activity at the network level in human hippocampus. Building on advances in culture techniques for maintaining viable human organotypic brain slices ex vivo, we evaluated the effectiveness of AAV-mediated delivery of inhibitory channelrhodopsins expressed in a subset of glutamatergic neurons to exert network level effects in hyperexcitable conditions. By integrating HD-MEA recordings with a custom system for optogenetic control, our experiments demonstrate a robust platform for high resolution analysis of network activity and cell type specific optogenetic manipulation in human hippocampus.

Optogenetics enables high spatiotemporal control over neural activity. Targeting local circuits has been shown to decrease epileptiform activity in non-human model systems10,11,20,21,56. but application of optogenetics to human neurons has been limited. Two studies have used patch-clamp recordings from single neurons to show excitatory optogenetic control of human neurons at a single cell level18,36. Hyperpolarizing, potassium-specific, kalium channelrhodopsins are a new tool in the optogenetic armamentarium40,41. Their inhibiting effects may be relevant to diseases of neuronal hyperactivity, such as epilepsy. This study demonstrates that optogenetic inhibition of human neurons can be used to modulate network-wide neuronal activity in human hippocampal slices.

The effects of optogenetic inhibition of glutamatergic CAMK2A+ neurons on network firing rates were more pronounced in the conditions of physiologic media and GABAAR blockade compared to low magnesium or kainic acid (Supplemental Fig. S3). Notably, the latter two conditions promote glutamate receptor activation. Optogenetic firing rate reductions in physiologic media and GABAAR blockade may be due to combined changes from HcKCR1-mediated inhibition of excitatory neurons, as well as indirect reductions in activity of their downstream neurons. In contrast, if low magnesium17 and kainic acid57 promote direct activation of glutamate receptors, the downstream effects of reducing spike activity in CAMK2A+ HcKCR1-expressing neurons may be less pronounced. This may also explain some persistence of epileptiform bursts during slice illumination with kainic acid media.

In our preparations, adding kainic acid to slices in low magnesium media resulted in rhythmic bursting events, consistent with prior studies22. This bursting activity appeared to be less common during optogenetic activation of HcKCR1, with none occurring during light-ON conditions in slice 11G (Extended Data Fig. 6g) and less common, but still present during 3 of 10 trials in slice 10F (Extended Data Fig. 6d). Incomplete silencing is not explained by transduction rate in these slices (Supplemental Fig. S2). This may also be related to the increased exogenous glutamatergic activation by kainic acid conditions discussed above. Further characterization of the rhythmic bursting observed is needed to understand effective methods for targeting this electrophysiologic phenotype. Interestingly, the observed results show remarkable similarity to in silico modeling (Extended Data Fig. 3), where coordinated activity was reduced in magnitude and frequency (but not completely extinguished) compared to control conditions.

Our in silico model is based on a recently described characterization of human hippocampal granule cell recordings.42 Since one limitation of human brain slice experiments is the scarcity of tissue specimens, this model allowed us to predict that even relatively low rates of transduction and inhibition of glutamatergic neurons could have network-wide effects without extensive tissue use. We envision that experimental design studies involving human tissue could involve an iterative framework involving biophysical models to predict cell type and network effects of perturbations, followed by experimentally testing and refinement. Advances in biophysical modeling of brain networks could thus significantly reduce overall needs for human tissue material42,58–61.

One notable aspect of the observed rhythmic bursting activity was the strong LFP coherence in the theta frequency band. Waves of coherence in the hippocampus, particularly in theta62, have been described in both human63–65 and non-human66–68 hippocampal preparations. HD-MEA recordings of this density have not been reported in the human hippocampus. This high level of resolution allowed for visualization of waves of theta phase-coherence across the GCL of the dentate gyrus (Fig. 4, Videos 3-4). This wave of propagation across the GCL is consistent with prior work showing that granule cells of the dentate gyrus receive a large amount of excitatory input, that is often phase-locked with theta frequency LFP69. Given evidence suggesting epileptiform discharges in the human brain are waves arising from an epileptogenic focus70, better characterization of such wave propagation may have significance for elucidating epileptic circuits. These data demonstrate the utility of the HD-MEA platform used here to characterize network synchronization patterns as a potential target for therapeutic intervention.

The ability to record dozens to hundreds of neurons simultaneously is one of the advantages of the HD-MEA recording platform described here. Such high-throughput methods may be effective for hypothesis generation about the neuronal ensemble and cell-type responses that can be validated with patch clamp or patch-seq71 based experiments. We used clustering techniques to leverage these advantages of the platform. We probed whether differences in neuronal cell type might contribute to differences in optogenetic response in our data, since many factors can affect neuronal responses, even to the same ligand72. The waveform clustering method distinguishes putative neuronal cell types based on extracellular spike-waveform features (Fig. 5)52,53. To test whether the clustering results were reasonable, we used the anatomic localization of our slice recordings. The granule cell layer is composed mostly of granule cell neurons, which are not typically found elsewhere in the hippocampus73–76. Comparing the distribution of waveform clusters from recordings over the GCL to recordings not over the GCL, 5 clusters were significantly associated with localization over the GCL (Fig. 5), suggesting these may represent GCL neurons.

We used an unsupervised clustering (HDBSCAN54,55,77,78) approach to distinguish patterns of neuronal response to optogenetic HcKCR1 activation that may not be captured by firing rate averages. Rather than simply clustering into responders and non-responders to slice illumination, this approach yielded 5 opto-response clusters (Fig. 6). The waveform clusters associated with GCL histologic localization (clusters 5, 6, 8, 9, 10 from Fig. 5) were overrepresented in opto-response cluster 3 (Supplemental Table ST6), which had on average a high baseline firing rate and modest reduction during slice illumination (Fig. 6 b&c). This suggested that cell-type—in this case granule cell identity—may play a role in optogenetic response to HcKCR1 activation, although activity-state at the time of slice-illumination cannot be ruled out based on these analyses40. Single nucleus sequencing data suggests that granule cells typically express CAMK2A at high levels compared to other hippocampal neurons79, such that promoter gene expression does not completely explain this modest reduction in firing rate seen during HcKCR1 activation in putative GCL neurons. These clustering techniques explain some of the heterogeneity of network and neuronal response to HcKCR1 activation in a subset of excitatory neurons, but there are limits on the conclusions that can be drawn from them. Our initial hypothesis was that the HDBSCAN analyses of firing rate response would yield two distinct clusters of responders and non-responders to light-ON conditions that might serve as a surrogate for HcKCR1-expression. The results, however, present a more complicated picture. Cell-type, HcKCR1-expression, and connectivity between neurons expressing and not expressing HcKCR1 are all likely contributing to the larger picture. Additional analyses of how individual neurons respond and influence one-another will be necessary to make conclusions of how manipulating a subset of neurons in a hippocampal slice affects network activity.

The present work utilizes hippocampi resected en bloc from patients with drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy. Clinically, these hippocampi have been determined to be likely or definitively involved in generating seizure activity. By this definition, the hippocampi recorded may have physiologic differences from what might be considered normal physiology or connectivity in non-epileptic human tissue. While this caveat should be noted when making biological conclusions about hippocampal function, it should also be noted that the intended target for prospective epilepsy therapies is epileptogenic hippocampi. This makes the preparation presented here an optimal model for pathologic insights, but perhaps limited in regard to normal hippocampal physiology.

Emerging strategies to develop AAVs with improved fidelity and robustness30 harness methods for screening synthetic libraries of capsid proteins, as well as enhancer elements29,30,80–82. AAV gene delivery studies have thus far focused on visualizing transduced neurons and describing their relevance with regard to normal CNS physiology32,80,83. Such investigations would benefit from characterizing how these tools can be utilized in pathologic circuits. Ex vivo cultures of human brain slices may both accelerate the development of such tools and serve as a platform for investigating the circuit-level effects of AAV-mediated, gain-of-function gene delivery. The techniques described herein allow for a layer of functional screening of AAVs for gene delivery by combining validation of human brain tissue expression with the potential to measure electrophysiologic activity and circuit-level effects.

The field of surgical treatment of epilepsy is evolving at a rapid pace. While surgical resection is the gold standard for drug-refractory focal epilepsy84, responsive neurostimulation is another increasingly common treatment for select patients85. Responsive neurostimulation involves running electrical current though neural tissue using stereotactically implanted electrodes. Neurostimulation techniques do confer clinical reductions in seizure frequency86, but the mechanism by which they modulate seizures is a topic of ongoing research87. Therapeutic translation of optogenetics for epilepsy is still theoretical88. The chronic effects and toxicity profiles of optogenetics in human hippocampal neurons require further study89. However, permanent implantation of electrodes and power-sources into patients with refractory epilepsy and other functional neurologic diseases is now routinely practiced90–97. Since such treatments are well-received by patients and clinicians, our working hypothesis is that the invasiveness of implanting a light guide and battery will not be the rate-limiting factor in developing therapeutic optogenetics. The lack of models for testing therapeutics in human tissue, on the other hand, may well impede progress on the many experimental fronts that would be necessary for moving in a translational direction88.

In conclusion, primary human tissue can serve as an experimental platform for optimizing and testing strategies to modulate network activity with the long-term goal of de-risking potential therapeutic interventions. Emerging technologies could enable rapid and scalable genetic access into cell types that could be tested in such ex vivo preparations. Here we describe a scenario whereby AAV-mediated delivery of inhibitory channelrhodopsin into a subset of glutamatergic neurons can be used to demonstrate network-wide activity modulation in human hippocampus. These techniques were previously relegated to animal modeling experiments. This study highlights the potential for human brain tissue to serve as a viable model for illuminating human brain neurophysiology.

### Design of optogenetic system

The purpose of the designed hardware platform is to trigger an optogenetic stimulation pulse and observe the response of neurons on a high-density electrode array. The optogenetic system was designed to be easy to replicate and does not require custom PCBs or soldering. Assembly instructions are available in Supplemental Data Fig. S1. The bill of materials with pricing is available in Supplemental Table ST1. Lid and insert from Figure 2 is described in detail in the Optogenetic 3D printed insert and lid section in Methods. Software will be provided in a GitHub repository upon release of the manuscript.

To run an experiment, the user must specify a calibration CSV file, which contains data on an LED’s power output (see Section Optogenetic power density measurement and calculation). The user also connects to the Arduino over a USB serial port. Afterward, the program creates a stimulation log CSV file into which the stimulation events with their parameters are recorded. Now, the user can construct their own stimulation sequences and use several helper functions with configurable stimulation pattern templates (Fig. 2f).

As the user runs the experiment, stimulation events are logged in both the stimulation log CSV file and the MaxWell voltage recording .hdf5 file. The MaxWell .hdf5 file has a field that stores a single bit value representing the GPIO pin signal (‘1’ for on, ‘0’ for off) for every frame of the recording (every 0.05 ms assuming 20kHz sampling). Therefore, we can extract at which recording frame the light turned on, and at which recording frame the light went back to being off. The CSV log file stores a timestamp of each event, as well as the intensity of light used and the duration of ON and OFF requested by the user.

### Optogenetic system software low-level functionality

The computer sends the Arduino an integer value over USB serial connection corresponding to the desired intensity. While the intensity is represented to the user as a decimal number between 0 and 1, it is converted to the nearest proportional integer in the range of the 12-bit DAC (0 to 4095). The range 0 to 4095 was chosen instead of the full 12-bit integer range 0 to 4096 because it more closely corresponded to 0 to 5V DAC output when measured on an oscilloscope.

The computer also sends the electrophysiology recording system a signal to set GPIO high. GPIO high is +2.0 – 3.3V, anything less or close to zero is considered GPIO low. When the GPIO signal is high, the Arduino sends a value to the DAC. Thus, to turn the light on, the computer needs to send a non-zero intensity value to the Arduino, and also trigger the recording system to set GPIO high.

### Activity detection algorithm and closed-loop optical intervention

We implemented an algorithm that monitors spike activity in real-time, using data from the HD-MEA (Fig. 3). This algorithm is meant to demonstrate a therapeutic use case scenario. When a pre-defined spike-threshold is detected, the algorithm triggers illumination of the slice. Spike activity was measured by counting the total number of 5-rms spikes that occurred in 10 seconds across all the electrodes on the HD-MEA.

Experimentally, this threshold was to be 2 to 4 times above the average baseline 5-rms spike activity for 1 minute prior to application of bicuculline. After the drug was applied, activity quickly surpassed this threshold. After the threshold is surpassed for a 10-second window, the algorithm triggers 10 seconds of illumination. Afterward, the algorithm goes back to monitoring activity. This algorithm is intentionally simple in nature, to provide a proof of concept that user-defined signals can be detected in real-time using HD-MEA interface with this this ex vivo model, in a closed-loop process.

### Data Acquisition

Neuronal activity was sampled simultaneously at 20kHz from multiple electrodes on the HD-MEA for both action potential and local field potential bandwidth. During the experiment, an activity scan assay using MaxLab Interface across all 26,400 electrodes was performed first, then a maximum of 1,024 available channels were manually selected to record from the most active areas spread across the MEA. Closed-loop seizure detection and optical intervention started after the assay from a custom Python script. After the experiment, raw activity data and optical stimulation timestamps were saved to an hdf5 file on local memory. The optical light protocol was written into a separate CSV logging file pairing with the raw data (see section Design of Optogenetic System).

### Spike Sorting

Kilosort298 was used for sorting the raw data into single unit activity. Since the high-density MEA can record one neuron from tens of channels, it is common that the spikes from many neurons overlap in time for a single channel. The template matching and clustering algorithm in Kilosort2 can distinguish spikes between different neurons based on their waveform and assign them to individual clusters. Raw data were bandpass filtered with 300 – 6000Hz and sorted in Kilosort2 with a voltage detection threshold of 6 RMS over the baseline. Spike sorting was performed on the Pacific Research Platform computing cluster with an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1080 Ti GPU. For spike sorting, both manual and auto-curation techniques were applied (see below). Kilosort2’s result was manually curated using Phy GUI99 by experienced electrophysiology researchers. The quality metrics100 for saving high-quality units are based on the shape of the spike waveform, firing rate, and interspike interval distribution.

We applied both auto-curation and manual curation to evaluate the integrity and physiologic relevance of each single unit output from spike sorting. We developed an auto-curation technique to allow for expedient curation of large numbers of units sometimes recorded on the HD-MEA. Comparing the results of auto-curation vs manual curation, we found auto-curation was in general more conservative (i.e. excluded more units). For auto-curation results that led to disparities from manually curated recordings (including slices 5C, 7D, 8D) we deferred to manual curation results to avoid under-sampling the network activity.

The manual curation process involved evaluating spike waveforms based on morphological characteristics and spatial distribution, calculating units minimum firing rates, and assessing interspike interval violation ratios. We check the morphology of the spike waveform and spatial distribution on the electrodes, preserving the high-quality waveform that follow the biophysical properties of an action potential generation, showcasing a reasonable duration, amplitude, a clear peak and trough, and exhibits coherent waveform patterns across neighboring channels relative to the unit’s identified location on the MEA.

The firing rate for each unit was calculated using the equation r a t e = N s p i k e s / T r e c where N s p i k e s represents the total number of spikes, and T r e c denotes the duration of the recording in seconds. Units that had less than 0.1 Hz firing rate were excluded from further analysis.

Additionally, interspike interval (ISI) violation ratio was assessed for each unit since it serves as an indicator of refractory period violation. The ISI violation ratio is defined as the total number of ISIs that are shorter than 1.5 ms relative to the total number of spikes. Units exhibiting more than a 10% ISI violation ratio were considered to have significant refractory period contamination and were thus removed from the dataset.

The auto-curation process is applied to the output of spike sorting by executing a Python script, as detailed in the associated GitHub repository: https://github.com/braingeneers/AndrewsGengVoitiukEtAl_SourceCode Within this script, we use curation functions from the SpikeInterface API curation module to evaluate quality metrics such as the Signal-to-Noise (SNR) ratio, ISI violation ratio, firing rate, and waveform spatial distribution for each unit. The SNR is determined using the compute_snrs function with a threshold set at 5 RMS. Calculation of the ISI violation ratio employs the Hill method101, facilitated by the compute_isi_violations function, with 1.5 ms as the threshold for identifying refractory period violations and a 20% violation rate for excluding a unit from further analysis. The firing rate threshold is 0.1 Hz. Waveforms are extracted for each unit across all active channels using the WaveformExtractor class, averaging up to 500 spikes. These waveforms are then sorted by amplitude. Units lacking coherent waveform patterns across the 8 nearest neighbor channels within a 17.5 um diameter are excluded.

### Propagation of Epileptiform Activity by Firing Rate

The propagation of epileptiform activity (Fig. 4c) is observed through an increase in firing rate during rhythmic bursting. For each individual unit, the baseline firing rate is determined by the number of regular spiking activities within the first 5 seconds of the recording. The increase in firing rate is assessed by comparing the spike activity during the burst against the baseline. To identify the burst period, the population firing rate of all units is measured in 100 ms continuous bins and smoothed with a Gaussian kernel (sigma = 5). The peak firing rate time point ( t p ) is determined using the SciPy function find_peaks, with a 2-second window centered around t p . Given the sequential nature of the units’ firing activity within the burst, this time window is further divided into 20 sub-windows of 100 ms each. A threshold set at 3 standard deviations above the baseline firing rate is applied to each unit within these sub-windows. The locations on the MEA of units surpassing this threshold are plotted, and the corresponding spike events are marked in red on the raster plot.

### Activity heatmaps

Activity heatmaps in Figure 1 and Figure 3 show the spatial distribution of significant voltage events. The MaxWell software computes a moving root-mean-square (rms) value for each electrode, and we used this to determine events that crossed a threshold set at 5x the rms value of each respective electrode. A 2D spatial grid of the counts per second was constructed, then a 2D Gaussian blur with radius was used to enable better visual continuity. Each position in the grid was divided by 2π2 so the values displayed would correspond to events per second, making it so the gaussian blur doesn’t significantly alter the values of each data point. These values were then plotted as the activity heatmaps, where warmer colors represent areas of higher event frequency, and darker colors denote regions with less activity.

### Statistics & Reproducibility

Sample sizes were maximized based on the availability of human brain tissue samples. There was no randomization. Samples were processed and experiments run in the order that patient tissue became available. No statistical method was used to predetermine sample size, but our sample sizes are similar to those reported in previous publications10,20,50. The experiments were not randomized. Data collection and analysis were not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments. Much of the statistical analyses involved comparing neuronal activity during a time period during which light was shone on the slice and comparing that data to periods of time immediately preceding and following this “light ON” time period. As such, knowing these exact time-points was necessary for accurate analysis. Data distribution was assumed to be normal, but this was not formally tested.

### Mean relative firing rate reduction

In Supplemental Fig. S3 we compare differences in magnitude of firing rate reduction from optogenetic activation between conditions exogenously increasing glutamatergic tone (low magnesium with and without kainic acid) vs those without exogenous glutamatergic tone (physiologic media with and without bicuculline). To do this, we calculated mean firing rates of all units during the 10s prior to light-ON and 10s during light-ON. For the low magnesium plus kainic acid (0-mg+KA), the same N=4 slices recorded for the 0-mg condition, using the recordings after administration of kainic acid.
